contrast: *Cunning* is not simple praise: it means clever in a sly, often dishonest way. For clever in a good sense say *smart* or *clever*. In older American books *cunning* can also mean *cute* (*a cunning little hat*).

senses.gloss: Clever at getting what you want, especially by tricking people.
examples: The villain in the movie is *cunning* and cruel.
They came up with a *cunning* plan to avoid paying taxes.
The fox is supposed to be the *most cunning* animal in the forest.

senses.gloss: Able to be cured.
examples: The disease is *curable* if it's caught early.
Doctors now treat it as a *curable* condition.
Skin cancer is *more curable* than many other cancers.

senses.gloss: Able to cure an illness, or meant to.
examples: Some people believe in the *curative* powers of honey.
The town was famous for its *curative* hot springs.
The treatment is not *curative*, but it eases the pain.

senses.gloss: Of milk or a sauce, separated into lumps, usually because it has gone sour or been overheated.
examples: The milk in the fridge was *curdled*.
Don't boil the sauce or you'll end up with a *curdled* mess.
The creamer came out *curdled*, so I threw it away.

senses.gloss: Of meat or fish, preserved by salting, smoking or drying.
examples: The deli sells Italian *cured* meats.
She served *cured* salmon on rye bread.
Bacon is *cured* pork belly.

senses.gloss: Healed of an illness, or free of a problem.
examples: After six months of treatment, she was completely *cured*.
I thought I was *cured* of my fear of flying, but I wasn't.

contrast: *Curly* hair grows that way; *curled* hair has been styled with an iron or rollers.

senses.gloss: Twisted into rings or curves, or bent into a round shape.
examples: She had long, *curled* hair for the wedding.
The cat lay *curled* up by the fire.
The old photo had *curled* edges.

contrast: It ends in -ly but is an adjective, not an adverb.

senses.gloss: Bad-tempered and easily annoyed, especially in an old person.
examples: Our *curmudgeonly* neighbor yells at kids who step on his lawn.
He's *curmudgeonly*, but he has a good heart.
My grandpa got *more curmudgeonly* every year.

comparison: not gradable — except sense 2: *more current*, *most current*
contrast: *Currently* is the adverb (*She currently lives in Denver*). *Current* is also a noun: *an electric current*, *an ocean current*. Russian *актуальный* is often *relevant* or *topical*, not *current*.

senses.gloss: Happening or existing now.
examples: What's your *current* address?
The *current* mayor took office in January.
Prices are high in the *current* economy.

senses.gloss: Up to date, or still valid.
examples: You need a *current* passport to fly.
Are you *current* on your rent?
This map is the *most current* one we have.

contrast: Before a noun it is often KUR-sid (*a cursed house*); in *cursed with* it is KURST. *Cursed* is also the past of the verb *curse* (*He cursed loudly*).

senses.gloss: Under a curse, so that bad things keep happening.
examples: The locals say the old house is *cursed*.
Some fans believe the team is *cursed*.
Nobody wanted to buy the *cursed* ring.

senses.gloss: Suffering from something bad that you cannot get rid of.
examples: She was *cursed* with terrible luck.
He's *cursed* with a bad back.

contrast: A false friend: *cursive* is joined-up handwriting, not *курсив*. Slanted print is *italics*. *Cursive* is also a noun: *Kids don't learn cursive anymore*.

senses.gloss: Of handwriting, with the letters joined together.
examples: Grandma's letters were written in beautiful *cursive* script.
She signed her name in *cursive* letters.
Many schools stopped teaching *cursive* handwriting.

senses.gloss: Done quickly, without much attention to detail.
examples: He gave the report only a *cursory* glance.
After a *cursory* search, the police left.
The inspection was *cursory* at best.

senses.gloss: Rudely short in speech or manner.
examples: She gave a *curt* reply and hung up.
He was *curt* with the waiter.
His emails got *more curt* as the deadline approached.

senses.gloss: Having attractive curves, usually said of a woman's body, sometimes of a car or other object.
senses.ru: с пышными формами, фигуристый, с плавными линиями
examples: The actress was known for her *curvaceous* figure.
The car's *curvaceous* body turned heads.
The new model is *more curvaceous* than the old boxy one.

senses.gloss: Having many curves or bends.
examples: We drove along a *curvy* mountain road.
The chair has a *curvy* back.
This is the *curviest* stretch of the highway.

senses.gloss: Of a woman, having a full figure with noticeable hips and breasts.
examples: The store sells jeans for *curvy* women.
She's *curvier* than her sister.

senses.gloss: Soft and padded, so it protects you from hard contact.
examples: The chairs have *cushioned* seats.
We sat on a *cushioned* bench by the window.
These running shoes are *more cushioned* than my old ones.

senses.gloss: Easy and comfortable, needing little effort; informal.
examples: He has a *cushy* job at his uncle's firm.
Life in the suburbs was pretty *cushy*.
She landed the *cushiest* assignment in the office.

ru: опекунский; связанный с содержанием под стражей; хозяйственный
contrast: In American English *custodian* is also the polite word for a janitor, so *custodial staff* are the people who clean a school or office.

senses.gloss: Having legal custody of a child.
examples: The *custodial* parent decides where the child goes to school.
She was granted *custodial* rights after the divorce.

senses.gloss: Involving being held in prison or by the police.
examples: The confession came during a *custodial* interrogation.
Several deaths in *custodial* settings are under investigation.

senses.gloss: Relating to cleaning and taking care of a building.
examples: The school hired more *custodial* staff.
*Custodial* services are included in the rent.

contrast: The noun *custom* means a tradition (*обычай*), and *customs* is the check at the border (*таможня*). The adjective *custom* is American; British English prefers *bespoke* or *made-to-measure*.

senses.gloss: Made or done to a particular customer's order.
examples: They have a *custom* kitchen with walnut cabinets.
The shop does *custom* paint jobs.
You can order *custom* T-shirts with your team's logo.

senses.gloss: Built to a particular customer's order.
examples: They live in a *custom-built* house by the lake.
His guitar was *custom-built* in Nashville.
The company makes *custom-built* computers for gamers.

senses.gloss: Made to a particular customer's order or measurements.
examples: He wore a *custom-made* suit to the wedding.
The boots were *custom-made* for her.
We ordered *custom-made* curtains for the big windows.

takes: *it is customary to* + infinitive; *for* someone *to* do

senses.gloss: Usual, according to custom or habit.
examples: It is *customary* to tip 15 to 20 percent in restaurants.
He took his *customary* seat at the end of the table.
In some cultures, it's *more customary* to bow than to shake hands.

comparison: not gradable — except sense 3, informally *more cut*
contrast: *He cut his hand* is the verb. In the muscle sense *cut* is informal American slang, like *ripped*.

senses.gloss: Removed from the plant by cutting.
examples: A vase of fresh *cut* flowers stood on the table.
The yard smelled of freshly *cut* grass.

senses.gloss: Shaped by cutting, like glass, a gem or a piece of clothing.
examples: The chandelier was made of *cut* crystal.
He wore a well-*cut* gray suit.
She wore a beautifully *cut* diamond.

senses.gloss: Having muscles that show clearly, with very little fat.
examples: He's been lifting weights, and he's really *cut*.
She got even *more cut* before the competition.

contrast: Mostly used with a negative: *It's not that cut-and-dried*. After a verb it is often written without hyphens: *The case is cut and dried*.

senses.gloss: Simple and clear, with no room for doubt or argument.
examples: The case isn't as *cut-and-dried* as it looks.
There's no *cut-and-dried* answer to that question.
For the judge, it was all pretty *cut-and-dried*.

senses.gloss: Sold at a reduced price, and often of low quality.
examples: They sell *cut-rate* airline tickets online.
He bought a *cut-rate* phone that broke in a week.
Don't trust a *cut-rate* contractor with your roof.

contrast: Said of an adult in American English, *cute* usually means *attractive* (*a cute guy*), not only sweet like a baby. Said with an edge (*Don't get cute with me*), it means too clever or cheeky.

senses.gloss: Pretty and charming, especially a baby, a small animal or a small thing.
examples: What a *cute* puppy!
That's the *cutest* baby I've ever seen.
Your little house is so *cute*.

senses.gloss: Sexually attractive.
examples: There's a *cute* guy in my chemistry class.
Do you think he's *cuter* than his brother?

senses.gloss: Clever in a way that is annoying or not quite honest.
examples: Don't get *cute* with me — just answer the question.
That was a *cute* trick, but it won't work twice.

senses.gloss: Ready to do anything to win, with no concern for others.
examples: They faced *cutthroat* competition from the big chains.
The restaurant business is *cutthroat*.
Wall Street was the *most cutthroat* place I've ever worked.

contrast: *A cutting* is also a noun: a piece cut from a plant to grow a new one. Don't confuse it with *cutting-edge*.

senses.gloss: Unkind and meant to hurt someone's feelings.
examples: She made a *cutting* remark about his weight.
His review of the film was *cutting*.
It was the *most cutting* thing anyone had ever said to her.

senses.gloss: Of wind or cold, sharp and unpleasant.
examples: A *cutting* wind blew off the lake.
The cold was *cutting* that morning.

contrast: Hyphenated as an adjective (*cutting-edge research*). *At the cutting edge of* is the noun phrase, with no hyphen.

senses.gloss: The newest and most advanced.
examples: The lab uses *cutting-edge* technology.
Their design is really *cutting-edge*.
It's the *most cutting-edge* phone on the market.

senses.gloss: Happening in cycles, repeating the same pattern again and again.
examples: The housing market is *cyclical*.
Some historians see a *cyclical* pattern in history.
Some industries are *more cyclical* than others.

senses.gloss: Shaped like a cylinder, long and round.
examples: The oil is stored in *cylindrical* tanks.
A soda can has a *cylindrical* shape.
The old water tower is *cylindrical*.

contrast: Partly a false friend. English *cynical* mostly means *distrustful, expecting the worst of people*. Russian *циничный* often suggests shameless or crude; for that, say *crude* or *shameless*.

senses.gloss: Believing that people act only out of selfishness, and distrusting their motives.
examples: Many voters are *cynical* about politicians.
After years in the news business, he became *more cynical*.
Don't be so *cynical* — some people really do want to help.

senses.gloss: Done for selfish reasons, with no concern for what is right.
examples: It was a *cynical* attempt to win votes.
The company made a *cynical* decision to hide the risks.

contrast: *A Cypriot* is also a person from Cyprus. The country is *Cyprus*.

senses.gloss: From or relating to Cyprus.
examples: Halloumi is a traditional *Cypriot* cheese.
Her mother is *Cypriot*.
The *Cypriot* government announced new rules for tourists.

contrast: Always with a capital *C*. It is also a noun: *Can you read Cyrillic?*

senses.gloss: Relating to the alphabet used for Russian, Ukrainian, Bulgarian, Serbian and other languages.
examples: Russian is written in the *Cyrillic* alphabet.
The sign was in *Cyrillic* letters, so I couldn't read it.
My keyboard has both Latin and *Cyrillic* characters.

contrast: Also spelled *tsarist*. It means *of the czars*, not *magnificent*: for *царский прием* say *a lavish welcome*.

senses.gloss: Relating to the czars or their government in Russia before 1917.
examples: The family fled *czarist* Russia in 1905.
Under *czarist* rule, most peasants could not read.
The museum has a collection of *czarist* coins.

contrast: Pronounced like *check*. The language is *Czech*, the people are *Czechs*, and the country is the *Czech Republic* or *Czechia*.

senses.gloss: From or relating to the Czech Republic, its people or its language.
examples: Prague is famous for *Czech* beer.
My grandparents were *Czech*.
She's taking a *Czech* class at the community college.

contrast: Historical: Czechoslovakia split into the Czech Republic and Slovakia in 1993. *Czechoslovak* means the same.

senses.gloss: From or relating to the former country of Czechoslovakia.
examples: He played on the *Czechoslovakian* national hockey team in the 1980s.
The film is a *Czechoslovakian* classic from the 1960s.
Her passport was still *Czechoslovakian* when she came to the U.S.

senses.gloss: Small, delicate and pretty.
examples: She wore *dainty* gold earrings.
They served *dainty* little sandwiches with the tea.
Her handwriting was *daintier* than mine.

senses.gloss: Harmed or broken, so it no longer works or looks as it should.
examples: The package arrived *damaged*.
The storm left dozens of *damaged* homes.
The *most damaged* buildings were near the coast.

senses.gloss: Emotionally hurt by bad experiences in the past.
examples: He was a *damaged* kid from a violent home.
She seemed deeply *damaged* by the divorce.

senses.gloss: Causing harm or damage.
examples: The scandal was *damaging* to her career.
Too much sun can have *damaging* effects on your skin.
The *most damaging* evidence came from his own emails.

contrast: A mild swear word: fine among friends, not in a job interview. *Damn* is also an adverb (*damn good*), an interjection (*Damn!*) and a noun (*I don't give a damn*). *Damned* means the same before a noun; *darn* is the polite version.

senses.gloss: Used before a noun to show anger or annoyance, or just for emphasis.
examples: The *damn* car won't start again.
Turn off that *damn* TV!
It's a *damn* shame they closed the old diner.

comparison: not gradable — except the idiom *damnedest* (*the damnedest thing* = the strangest)
contrast: Stronger than *darned*, about as strong as *damn*. *The damned* (noun) are the souls in hell. *I'll be damned!* shows surprise; *I'll be damned if I pay that* means *I refuse to*. *Damned good* is the adverb.

senses.gloss: Used before a noun to show anger or annoyance, or just for emphasis.
examples: The *damned* printer is jammed again.
I can't find my *damned* phone.
It was the *damnedest* thing — the dog opened the door by itself.

senses.gloss: Condemned to hell, or certain to fail whatever you do.
examples: They believed the souls of sinners were *damned* forever.
You're *damned* if you do and *damned* if you don't.

senses.gloss: Showing clearly that someone has done something wrong.
examples: The report contains *damning* evidence against the company.
The video was *damning*.
The *most damning* testimony came from his former assistant.

contrast: Russian *влажный* has three English partners: *damp* (a little wet, often unpleasant: *a damp basement*), *moist* (pleasantly: *moist cake*) and *humid* (air and weather).

senses.gloss: Slightly wet, often in an unpleasant way.
examples: Wipe the table with a *damp* cloth.
The basement always feels cold and *damp*.
My towel was even *damper* the next morning.

senses.gloss: Of music, with a rhythm that is good for dancing.
examples: The band plays upbeat, *danceable* music.
The song is catchy and *danceable*.
Her new album is *more danceable* than the last one.

position: both — mostly after a verb, in *fine and dandy* and *just dandy*
contrast: Old-fashioned and often ironic today: *Oh, that's just dandy* means *that's terrible*. *A dandy* (noun) is a man who cares a lot about his clothes.

senses.gloss: Very good; often used ironically to mean the opposite.
examples: Everything is fine and *dandy* here.
We missed the flight? Well, that's just *dandy*.
Grandpa thought it was a *dandy* idea.

senses.gloss: Likely to cause harm, injury or death.
examples: It's *dangerous* to swim here after dark.
Smoking is *dangerous* to your health.
This is the *most dangerous* road in the state.

contrast: In slang, *dank* means *excellent* (*dank memes*); it is informal and mostly online.

senses.gloss: Unpleasantly cold, wet and smelling of mold.
examples: The prisoners were kept in a *dank* cell.
The cabin smelled *dank* after the rainy winter.
The basement was the *dankest* room in the house.

senses.gloss: Of a man, neat, well-dressed and stylish.
examples: He looked *dapper* in his navy suit.
A *dapper* old man tipped his hat to us.
You look even *more dapper* with the beard.

senses.gloss: Marked with patches of light and shade, or with spots of color.
senses.ru: пятнистый, в пятнах света и тени
examples: We walked through the *dappled* shade of the forest.
She rode a *dappled* gray horse.
The garden was *dappled* with sunlight.

senses.gloss: Brave and willing to take risks.
examples: Firefighters made a *daring* rescue from the roof.
She's *more daring* than her brother.
It was a *daring* plan, and it worked.

senses.gloss: New or shocking, and likely to upset some people.
examples: The designer showed some *daring* outfits.
The film was considered *daring* for its time.

senses.gloss: Having dark hair.
examples: A tall, *dark-haired* woman opened the door.
Both of their kids are *dark-haired*.
They're looking for a *dark-haired* actor to play the son.

senses.gloss: Having dark skin.
examples: Her father was *dark-skinned* and had curly hair.
The makeup brand offers shades for *dark-skinned* women.
*Darker-skinned* people can still get sunburned.

senses.gloss: Made dark, or with the lights turned off.
examples: We sat in the *darkened* theater waiting for the movie.
She walked down the *darkened* hallway.
The house stood *darkened* and silent.

contrast: Mostly a noun used to address someone (*Thanks, darling*). As an adjective it sounds a little old-fashioned or gushing.

senses.gloss: Much loved.
examples: She dedicated the book to her *darling* husband.
Our *darling* daughter turns five today.

senses.gloss: Very pretty or charming.
examples: What a *darling* little dress!
Isn't that cottage just *darling*?
It's the *most darling* shop in town.

comparison: not gradable — except the idiom *darnedest* (*the darnedest things*)
contrast: A polite American way to avoid *damned*. *Darned good* is the adverb. *Darned socks* are mended ones, from the verb *darn*.

senses.gloss: Used to show annoyance or surprise, or just for emphasis, without swearing.
examples: The *darned* dog got out again.
Well, I'll be *darned* — you were right.
Kids say the *darnedest* things.

senses.gloss: Relating to Charles Darwin or his theory of evolution.
examples: The course covers *Darwinian* evolution.
He explained the idea in *Darwinian* terms.

senses.gloss: Brutally competitive, so that only the strongest survive.
examples: Silicon Valley can be a *Darwinian* place.
The airline industry is *Darwinian*: the weak go bankrupt.

senses.gloss: Attractive and stylish in a confident, exciting way, usually said of a man.
examples: A *dashing* young officer asked her to dance.
He looked *dashing* in his tuxedo.
He was the *most dashing* man at the party.

contrast: Old-fashioned and now often humorous (*a dastardly plot*). It ends in -ly but is an adjective.

senses.gloss: Evil and cruel in a cowardly way.
examples: It was a *dastardly* attack on innocent people.
The cartoon villain twirled his mustache and made *dastardly* plans.
He's the *most dastardly* character in the book.

contrast: Not *датированный*: in *a letter dated May 5*, *dated* is the verb *date*. The adjective means old-fashioned.

senses.gloss: Old-fashioned, belonging to an earlier time.
examples: The kitchen looks a little *dated*.
Some of the jokes in the movie feel *dated* now.
Of all the rooms, the bathroom looked the *most dated*.

form: -ing from *daunt* — what makes you lose confidence

senses.gloss: Seeming difficult or frightening, so that you lose confidence.
examples: Moving to a new country can be *daunting*.
She faced the *daunting* task of rebuilding the company.
The *most daunting* part was speaking in front of 500 people.

senses.gloss: One day old; of food, not fresh because it was made the day before.
examples: The bakery sells *day-old* bread at half price.
The farm sells *day-old* chicks in the spring.
I'm not drinking *day-old* coffee.

contrast: Hyphenated before a noun. Without hyphens it is usually an adverb phrase: *We live day to day*.

senses.gloss: Happening every day as part of normal life or work.
examples: She handles the *day-to-day* running of the office.
Stress is part of my *day-to-day* life.
The manager deals with *day-to-day* problems.

senses.gloss: Lasting all day.
examples: The museum is hosting a *daylong* festival.
Teachers attended a *daylong* training session.
After a *daylong* search, they found the missing hiker.

senses.gloss: Unable to think clearly, because of a blow, a shock or tiredness.
examples: He looked *dazed* after hitting his head.
Survivors wandered the streets, *dazed* and confused.
She walked out of the meeting with a *dazed* expression.

senses.gloss: So bright that you cannot see well for a moment.
examples: The *dazzling* sun reflected off the snow.
The lights on stage were *dazzling*.

senses.gloss: Extremely impressive or beautiful.
examples: She gave a *dazzling* performance.
The team's *dazzling* play won the crowd over.
It was the *most dazzling* smile I'd ever seen.

contrast: Also an adverb: *The country is de facto split in two*.

senses.gloss: Existing in fact, even if not officially or legally.
examples: English is the *de facto* language of international business.
He became the *de facto* leader of the group.
The river is now the *de facto* border between the two regions.

senses.gloss: Existing by law or officially.
examples: The South had *de jure* segregation until the 1960s.
The country won *de jure* independence in 1991.
His power was *de jure*, but his deputy made the real decisions.

senses.gloss: Required by fashion, custom or good manners.
examples: A black tie is *de rigueur* at the gala.
Hoodies and sneakers are *de rigueur* in tech offices.
For a while, the man bun was a *de rigueur* look in Brooklyn.

contrast: The preposition changes the meaning: *dead set against* = strongly opposed; *dead set on* = determined to do or get it.

senses.gloss: Completely opposed to something.
examples: My parents were *dead set* against the move.
The mayor is *dead set* against raising taxes.

senses.gloss: Completely determined to do or get something.
examples: She's *dead set* on going to law school.
He was *dead set* on buying that truck.

contrast: The noun is two words with no hyphen: *The road is a dead end*.

senses.gloss: Offering no chance of progress or a better future.
examples: He was stuck in a *dead-end* job.
She finally left her *dead-end* relationship.

senses.gloss: Of a street, closed at one end.
examples: We live on a quiet *dead-end* street.
The *dead-end* road stops at the river.

contrast: Also an adverb, usually without the hyphen: *The clock is dead on time*.

senses.gloss: Exactly right.
examples: Your impression of the boss is *dead-on*.
Her prediction turned out to be *dead-on*.
He gave a *dead-on* description of the suspect.

senses.gloss: Unable to reach an agreement or a decision.
examples: The jury was *deadlocked* after three days.
Talks between the union and the company remain *deadlocked*.
The *deadlocked* Senate could not pass the budget.

contrast: Also an adverb: *She said it deadpan*.

senses.gloss: Funny while showing no emotion and looking completely serious.
examples: He has a *deadpan* sense of humor.
Her delivery was completely *deadpan*.
His *deadpan* expression made the joke even funnier.

senses.gloss: Extremely loud.
examples: The music at the club was *deafening*.
There was a *deafening* explosion.
When he finished speaking, the silence was *deafening*.

contrast: In British English *dear* also means *expensive*; Americans say *expensive*. *Oh dear!* is an interjection, and *dear* is also used to address someone (*Thanks, dear*).

senses.gloss: Loved very much, or very important to someone.
examples: She's a *dear* friend of mine.
The house was very *dear* to him.
My *dearest* wish is to see my family again.

senses.gloss: Used before a name or title at the start of a letter or email.
examples: *Dear* Mr. Johnson, thank you for your letter.
She began the email with *Dear* Team.

senses.gloss: Sweet and kind; a little old-fashioned.
examples: Your grandmother is such a *dear* woman.
The Hendersons are *dear* people.

contrast: In *deathly pale* and *deathly quiet*, *deathly* is an adverb meaning *extremely*. Don't confuse it with *deadly*: *a deadly disease* is one that kills.

senses.gloss: Like death, for example in its silence, stillness or paleness.
examples: A *deathly* silence fell over the room.
Her face had a *deathly* pallor.
The empty streets had a *deathly* stillness.

senses.gloss: Made lower in quality, value or moral standards.
examples: Critics say reality TV has created a *debased* culture.
The old coins were made of *debased* silver.
The word has become *debased* through overuse.

senses.gloss: Not certain, so people may have different opinions about it.
examples: It's *debatable* whether the new law helped anyone.
That's a *debatable* point.
Whether it was worth the money is even *more debatable*.

form: -ed from *debilitate* — the person who is weakened
contrast: *Debilitated* describes the weakened person; *debilitating* describes the illness or thing that weakens them.

senses.gloss: Very weak, especially because of illness.
examples: The patient was *debilitated* after months of chemotherapy.
They cared for *debilitated* elderly relatives at home.
He seemed *more debilitated* each time I visited.

senses.gloss: Making someone very weak or unable to live normally.
examples: She suffers from *debilitating* migraines.
The disease can be *debilitating*.
Fatigue is one of the *most debilitating* symptoms.

senses.gloss: Stylish, confident and charming, usually said of a man.
examples: He was a *debonair* man in a white dinner jacket.
The actor looked *debonair* on the red carpet.
He's even *more debonair* in person.

senses.gloss: Having low moral standards and caring too much about pleasure.
examples: Critics attacked the *decadent* lifestyle of the rich.
The empire grew weak and *decadent*.

senses.gloss: Very rich and enjoyable, in a way that feels like a luxury.
examples: We shared a *decadent* chocolate cake.
Breakfast in bed felt wonderfully *decadent*.
It's the *most decadent* dessert on the menu.

senses.gloss: Rotten or falling apart because of natural processes.
examples: The dentist pulled a *decayed* tooth.
They found the *decayed* remains of an old boat.
The wood near the bottom was badly *decayed*.

contrast: *Deceitful* describes a person who lies and tricks; *deceptive* describes something that gives a false impression. Russian *обманчивый* is usually *deceptive*.

senses.gloss: Lying to or tricking people.
examples: Her *deceitful* behavior cost her the job.
He was *deceitful* with everyone, even his wife.
He was the *most deceitful* person I've ever worked with.

senses.gloss: With power or control spread among many places or people rather than one center.
examples: The U.S. has a *decentralized* school system.
Bitcoin is a *decentralized* currency.
The company became *more decentralized* after the merger.

contrast: *Deceptive* describes things that give a false impression; *deceitful* describes people who lie.

senses.gloss: Giving a false impression, whether on purpose or not.
examples: Appearances can be *deceptive*.
The company was fined for *deceptive* advertising.
The *most deceptive* part of the hike is the last mile, which looks flat but isn't.

contrast: Not *решённый*: *The matter is decided* is the verb. Before a noun, *decided* means clear and definite. The adverb *decidedly* (*decidedly odd*) is more common.

senses.gloss: Clear and definite; easy to notice.
examples: The home team has a *decided* advantage.
There was a *decided* change in his attitude.
She speaks with a *decided* Southern accent.

contrast: *Deciding* is the one thing that settles a result (*the deciding goal*). *Decisive* can mean that too, but it also describes a person who decides quickly.

senses.gloss: Settling the result of a vote, a game or a choice.
examples: The senator cast the *deciding* vote.
Price was the *deciding* factor.
They won the *deciding* game of the series.

senses.gloss: Of a tree or bush, losing its leaves every fall.
examples: Oaks and maples are *deciduous* trees.
In the fall, the *deciduous* forests turn red and gold.
Most of the shrubs in our yard are *deciduous*.

contrast: Americans write a decimal point, not a comma: *3.5*, said *three point five*. *A decimal* is also a noun.

senses.gloss: Based on the number ten.
examples: Move the *decimal* point two places to the right.
The metric system is a *decimal* system.
Round the answer to two *decimal* places.

senses.gloss: Having a strong effect on the result.
examples: It was a *decisive* victory for the Democrats.
The Battle of Midway was *decisive* in the Pacific war.

senses.gloss: Able to make decisions quickly and firmly.
examples: We need a *decisive* leader.
She's *more decisive* than her boss.
Be *decisive* — the offer won't last.

senses.gloss: Stated officially or publicly.
examples: She is a *declared* candidate for governor.
His *declared* goal is to cut taxes.
The country has been in a *declared* state of emergency since June.

senses.gloss: No longer secret, so the public can see it.
examples: Historians studied *declassified* CIA files.
A *declassified* memo shows the president knew about the plan.
The report is now *declassified* and available online.

senses.gloss: Made more attractive with added things.
examples: The cake was beautifully *decorated*.
Ours was the *most decorated* house on the block at Christmas.

senses.gloss: Having received medals or other honors.
examples: He is a highly *decorated* war veteran.
She's the *most decorated* gymnast in U.S. history.

senses.gloss: Meant to look attractive rather than to be useful.
examples: She bought some *decorative* pillows for the couch.
The fireplace is only *decorative*; it doesn't work.
The new design is *more decorative* than practical.

senses.gloss: Polite and correct in behavior; formal.
examples: The guests were quiet and *decorous*.
They exchanged a *decorous* kiss on the cheek.
The ceremony was *more decorous* than the party that followed.

senses.gloss: Smaller in amount, level or number than before.
examples: Side effects include *decreased* appetite.
Exercise is linked to a *decreased* risk of heart disease.
Workers reported *decreased* stress after the change.

senses.gloss: Old and in bad condition, or weak because of old age.
examples: They bought a *decrepit* old farmhouse and fixed it up.
The *decrepit* bus broke down twice on the way.
The building looked even *more decrepit* in daylight.

contrast: After *dedicated to*, use a noun or *-ing*, not an infinitive: *dedicated to helping*, not *dedicated to help*.

senses.gloss: Working hard at something because you believe it is important.
examples: She's a *dedicated* teacher.
He is *dedicated* to helping homeless veterans.
No one on the team is *more dedicated* than Mike.

senses.gloss: Made or used for one particular purpose only.
examples: The hospital has a *dedicated* children's ward.
We run the website on a *dedicated* server.
